source.title: Reawakening knowledge: Anticipatory recovery from catastrophic interference via structured training
source.authors: Yanlai Yang; Matt Jones; M. Mozer; Mengye Ren

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports model-size effects on anticipatory recovery during cyclic fine-tuning, not the held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Hoffmann et al. [5] as background on LLM training, but does not test or rely on the stated scaling-law claim. Its cross-entropy results concern cyclic fine-tuning on documents also used for evaluation; the model-size result concerns recovery scores, not power-law loss scaling. The recovery-score size sweep is recorded as a related finding that fits no claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper studies anticipatory recovery in cyclic fine-tuning; it cites Hoffmann et al. only as background on online LLM training. No held-out pretraining loss vs scale, compute-optimal allocation, shape-at-fixed-parameters, or downstream-scaling result is reported. Model-size effects concern recovery score, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLMs fine-tuned cyclically show anticipatory recovery from forgetting. It emerges only with sufficient width and depth, strengthens with model size, and depends on how well the model fits each document. It also appears in some vision models, and cyclic ordering beats shuffling in prequential (online) loss. They draw no conclusions about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates cyclic fine-tuning and anticipatory recovery rather than the scaling-law measurement or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery is reported to vary with model size and with training factors including gradient steps, context length, frozen blocks, optimizer, data randomness, and initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: In cyclic fine-tuning, larger pre-trained Pythia models (160M to 2.8B) show stronger anticipatory recovery, with a sharp jump from 160M to 410M. Randomly initialized models show the same size trend, more weakly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Anticipatory recovery during cyclic fine-tuning emerges and strengthens with model capacity.

record.code_released: Code and reproduction instructions are stated to be in the supplementary material; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The LLM experiments use the same documents for fine-tuning and evaluation, and the authors note that ablations were run in only a single setting. The recovery-score size results are plotted without numeric values in the text. These results do not assess the scaling-law claim.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were reported. Other unrelated cyclic-training results, including the random-initialization size comparison and online-loss comparison, were not cataloged.

untested.parts: Loss vs depth/width at fixed parameter count. Width/depth sweeps (Fig. 3) vary parameter count and measure recovery, not loss at fixed size.
Power-law loss in other modalities or regimes. Vision and fine-tuning experiments measure recovery, not scaling form.
Downstream performance vs scale or loss.
Fit/setup dependence of exponents or allocation.

record.verdict_notes: Changed relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': Hoffmann et al. appears only as a background citation. Table 1 reports online loss by model size (410M–2.8B). It is not monotone in size and is fine-tuning loss on the training documents, not held-out pretraining loss, so it does not bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Loss comparisons across depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting/setup choices, and departures from a single power law.
